title: Cyber law draft halves rumour penalty; public comments due 25 Nov
excerpt: NGOs and rights groups have until 25 November to comment. Critics say blocking powers and broad offences remain.
content:
The government has published a revised draft of the Cyber Security (Amendment) Act 2026 that cuts the maximum prison term for spreading rumours or disinformation from 10 years to five, and is taking public comments until 25 November, The Daily Star and Prothom Alo reported on 13 November. The Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Division put the draft on its website on 10 November, according to The Daily Star.

What the new draft changes

  • Rumours and disinformation (Section 26A): up to five years in prison, a Tk 10 lakh fine, or both, down from 10 years and Tk 40 lakh. The offence now covers deliberately spreading false or distorted information that causes public panic, agitation or social unrest. It stays cognisable and non-bailable.
  • Defamation: up to two years and Tk 5 lakh, following the Penal Code definition, according to Prothom Alo. It is bailable and non-cognisable.
  • Belittling or bullying: up to three years and Tk 5 lakh, cognisable and non-bailable, The Daily Star reported. Prothom Alo said distorted memes and caricatures made to mock someone are included.
  • Registered media: tribunal approval would be needed before an arrest over news, opinion, pictures or cartoons in registered media (Section 46A), and outlets would get 15 days' written notice before proceedings (Section 29).

What stays

  • Blocking content: agencies could still block or remove content without tribunal approval. People affected must be told the reason within three days and can ask the National Cyber Security Agency to restore it, with a decision due in 15 days.
  • Search and arrest: Sections 33 to 35 on searches, seizures and warrantless action are unchanged.
  • Immunity: members and officials of the Cyber Protection Council would be protected from cases for acts done in good faith, and the council would meet twice a year instead of quarterly, The Daily Star reported.

What critics said

Dr Iftekharuzzaman, executive director of Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB), told The Daily Star: "The draft CPA was conceptually faulty to begin with, and now this new draft is even constitutionally flawed." He said protections for media alone were discriminatory. Human Rights Support Society (HRSS) asked for clearer definitions, bailable offences, civil remedies for defamation and judicial approval for blocking.

Kamal Ahmed, consulting editor of The Daily Star and former head of the Media Reform Commission, told Prothom Alo that the changes were not enough and that the safeguards should cover ordinary citizens, not only registered media.

Why it matters

NGOs, rights groups and community organisations post reports, case studies and criticism online every day. Broad offences such as causing "public panic" and blocking without a court order can be used against advocacy and whistleblowing, as the repealed Digital Security Act was. The comment period is a chance for the sector to put its concerns on record before the bill goes to Parliament.

What to watch

Submissions from NGO networks, journalist bodies and rights groups before 25 November, and whether the ICT Division publishes a further revision before the bill is tabled. Devlens covered the previous draft on 8 November.
